---
title: "Adding to the plot and saving"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5,
  out.width = "100%",
  dpi = 150,
  dev = "ragg_png"
)
```

```{r setup}
library(forestmap)
```

The plot is made with ggplot2 and patchwork, so you can add titles, lines
and scales of your own. This page also shows how to save it. All the examples use the `forestmap_example` data that comes with the
package.

## Adding to the plot

`plot_forestmap()` returns a [patchwork](https://patchwork.data-imaging.com)
of ggplot2 plots: `p[[1]]` is the forest plot and `p[[2]]` the heatmap. (With
`continuous_range = "legend"`, `p[[3]]` holds the legends.)
You can add to either one.

### Title and caption

```{r, fig.height = 5}
p <- plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c("Population" = "population", "Study design" = "design")
)

p + patchwork::plot_annotation(
  title = "Effects of the intervention",
  subtitle = "60 studies, sorted by effect size",
  caption = "Simulated data"
)
```

### Show the pooled effect

Add a line to the forest plot, for example at the pooled effect from your
meta-analysis. Here it's a simple inverse-variance (fixed-effect) average:

```{r}
pooled <- weighted.mean(forestmap_example$smd, w = 1 / forestmap_example$vi)

p <- plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c("Population" = "population", "Study design" = "design")
)

p[[1]] <- p[[1]] +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = pooled, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.4) +
  ggplot2::annotate(
    "text", x = 1, y = pooled, label = "Pooled effect",
    hjust = 0, vjust = -0.6, size = 3, family = "Roboto Condensed"
  )
p
```

Text added with `annotate()` doesn't pick up the plot's font automatically,
so set `family` to the font the plot uses (`"Roboto Condensed"` unless you
chose another).

### Axis breaks

Change where the y-axis labels go with `scale_y_continuous()`. Use round
numbers; `seq()` can create tiny rounding errors that show up as odd labels:

```{r}
p <- plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c("Population" = "population", "Study design" = "design")
)

p[[1]] <- p[[1]] + ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(-1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1))
p
```

## Saving

`plot_forestmap()` doesn't save anything; use `ggplot2::ggsave()` and choose
the size there. The plot looks best at around 7 × 5 inches with four
properties; add height as you add rows.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
ggplot2::ggsave("forestmap.png", p, width = 7, height = 5.25, dpi = 300)
ggplot2::ggsave("forestmap.svg", p, width = 7, height = 5.25)
ggplot2::ggsave("forestmap.pdf", p, width = 7, height = 5.25, device = cairo_pdf)
```

For PDFs, use `device = cairo_pdf`. PDFs (and RStudio's Plots pane) only see
fonts installed on your computer, so install Roboto Condensed (from
`system.file("fonts", package = "forestmap")`) or choose an installed font.
In RStudio you can instead set *Tools > Global Options > General >
Graphics > Backend* to **AGG**.
